title: New surveillance tech links your phone to your license plate
summary: SignalTrace, a surveillance system developed by Leonardo, correlates wireless device signals (e.g., phones, smartwatches) with license plate data to track recurring patterns of movement. While the system does not directly identify individuals, it enables law enforcement to infer associations and identities by linking anonymous device signals to known vehicles or locations. This raises privacy concerns, as mobility data can uniquely identify individuals and reveal personal relationships, even without explicit identifiers like names.
key_points: SignalTrace pairs automatic license plate readers with sensors detecting wireless device signals (e.g., Bluetooth, RFID) to create electronic signatures of recurring movement patterns.
The system does not directly identify individuals but associates anonymous device signals with license plates, enabling indirect identification through investigative methods.
Privacy risks arise because mobility data (e.g., 4 time-and-place points) can uniquely identify 95% of individuals, per research in *Scientific Reports*.
Legal precedents like *Carpenter v. United States* and *Chatrie v. United States* highlight Fourth Amendment concerns over location tracking and inferred associations.

SignalTrace shifts surveillance focus from known identities to patterns of movement and proximity, potentially revealing social ties (e.g., friendships, protests) without direct evidence of wrongdoing.
The system is marketed as a lead-generation tool for law enforcement, but its use of relational inference raises ethical and legal questions about indirect identification.
